subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast
Response to exercise and oxygen debt

questions.q: Which word equation correctly represents photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide + water into glucose + oxygen. The light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts.

questions.q: Photosynthesis is described as an endothermic reaction because:
options: Energy is transferred from the environment (light) to the plant
It releases heat energy to the surroundings
questions.explain: Photosynthesis is endothermic: energy is transferred from the environment into the chloroplasts by light. This energy is stored in the glucose that is made.

questions.q: Where in a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy. Palisade mesophyll cells near the top of the leaf have many chloroplasts.

questions.q: Which of these is a limiting factor for the rate of photosynthesis?
options: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature
Amount of nitrogen in the soil
questions.explain: The rate of photosynthesis can be limited by light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature and (indirectly) the amount of chlorophyll. Whichever is in shortest supply limits the rate.

questions.q: On a graph, the rate of photosynthesis increases as light intensity increases, then levels off. What does the plateau indicate?
options: Light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor (e.g. CO2 or temperature) now limits the rate
questions.explain: When the graph plateaus, increasing light no longer increases the rate, so light is no longer limiting. Another factor such as CO2 concentration or temperature has become the limiting factor.

questions.q: How could a farmer increase photosynthesis in a greenhouse in winter?
options: Keep the plants in the dark
Add artificial lighting, extra CO2 and heating
questions.explain: Growers can boost photosynthesis and yield by increasing light (artificial lighting), CO2 concentration and temperature to optimum levels. This is more expensive, so they must balance cost against extra yield.

questions.q: Which is NOT a use of the glucose made in photosynthesis?
options: Used in respiration to release energy
Absorbed directly from the soil by roots
Used to make cellulose for cell walls
questions.explain: Glucose from photosynthesis is used in respiration, stored as starch, converted to fats/oils, used to make cellulose, and combined with nitrate ions to make amino acids. It is not absorbed from the soil.

questions.q: Plants convert some glucose and nitrate ions absorbed from the soil into which substances?
questions.explain: Glucose is combined with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to make amino acids, which are then used to make proteins for growth.

questions.q: In the required practical using pondweed, how can the rate of photosynthesis be measured?
options: By counting the number of leaves
By counting bubbles of oxygen (or measuring gas volume) produced per minute
questions.explain: The rate can be measured by counting the oxygen bubbles released per minute (or collecting the gas). Moving the lamp closer/further changes light intensity. Rate is proportional to 1/distance squared (inverse square law).

questions.q: If a lamp is moved from 20 cm to 10 cm from the pondweed, what happens to the light intensity? (inverse square law)
questions.explain: Light intensity is proportional to 1 / distance squared. Halving the distance (from 20 cm to 10 cm) increases the intensity by about four times, so the rate of photosynthesis rises (if light is limiting).

questions.q: Which word equation represents aerobic respiration?
questions.explain: Aerobic respiration is glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water. It occurs continuously in the mitochondria and transfers the energy the organism needs.

questions.q: Respiration is described as an exothermic reaction because it:
options: Transfers energy to the environment (releases energy)
questions.explain: Respiration is exothermic: it transfers (releases) energy from glucose. This energy is used for movement, keeping warm, building larger molecules and active transport.

questions.q: What is the product of anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells?
questions.explain: In muscle cells, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid: glucose -> lactic acid. It releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration because glucose is not fully oxidised.

questions.lo: Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast
questions.q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells (fermentation) produces:
questions.explain: Anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. This fermentation is important in making bread (CO2 makes it rise) and alcoholic drinks (ethanol).

questions.q: Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy than aerobic respiration per glucose molecule?
options: The oxidation of glucose is incomplete
It happens at a higher temperature
questions.explain: Anaerobic respiration is the incomplete oxidation of glucose, so much less energy is transferred per glucose molecule than in aerobic respiration, which fully oxidises glucose to CO2 and water.

questions.lo: Response to exercise and oxygen debt
questions.q: During vigorous exercise, why does the heart rate and breathing rate increase?
options: To supply more oxygenated blood to muscles and remove CO2
To lower the body temperature only
questions.explain: During exercise, breathing and heart rate increase to supply muscles with more oxygenated blood and glucose for aerobic respiration, and to remove carbon dioxide. Muscle stores of glycogen are also converted to glucose.

questions.lo: Response to exercise and oxygen debt
questions.q: What is the oxygen debt built up during vigorous exercise? (Higher tier)
options: The extra oxygen needed after exercise to remove the accumulated lactic acid
The oxygen stored in the muscles at rest
The oxygen used to make glucose
questions.explain: Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with and break down the lactic acid that built up from anaerobic respiration. Blood transports lactic acid to the liver.

questions.q: What is meant by metabolism?
options: The sum of all the chemical reactions in a cell or the body
questions.explain: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions in a cell or the body. It includes reactions that build larger molecules (e.g. starch, cellulose, proteins) and those that break molecules down.

questions.q: Which is an example of a metabolic reaction that builds up a larger molecule?
options: Digestion of fats to fatty acids
Formation of starch from glucose molecules
questions.explain: Building starch, glycogen and cellulose from glucose, and forming lipids from glycerol and fatty acids, are metabolic reactions that make larger molecules. Respiration and digestion break molecules down.

questions.q: In the liver, what happens to excess amino acids that cannot be stored? (Higher tier)
options: They are turned back into glucose only
They are excreted unchanged in sweat
They are stored as fat directly
They are deaminated to form ammonia, which is converted to urea for excretion
questions.explain: Excess amino acids undergo deamination in the liver to form ammonia (toxic), which is then converted to urea and safely excreted by the kidneys in urine.
